pedagogy.summary: Estimating angles is the sense-making partner of protractor measuring: the child judges an angle's size in degrees WITHOUT a tool, by comparing it against internalised benchmark angles (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). The pedagogical goal is a stable mental image of a right angle and a half/three-quarter turn, so that any angle can be placed relative to them ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°'). This extends the acute/obtuse vocabulary to REFLEX angles (between 180° and 360°), which children meet here for the first time and which the semicircular protractor cannot directly read. Estimation is what makes measuring self-correcting: a child who expects 'about 130°' will not accept a protractor read of 50°.
bestPractices: Anchor a small set of benchmark angles as physical/mental images first — the right angle (corner, quarter turn), the straight angle (180°), 45° as half a right angle, 270° as three right angles — then estimate everything by comparison to the nearest benchmark.
Always estimate BEFORE measuring, then measure to check; treat a big estimate-vs-measure gap as a signal to recheck placement, not to discard the estimate.
Introduce reflex angles explicitly as 'more than a straight line, less than a full turn' and estimate them as 360° minus the smaller angle, since a semicircular protractor reads only to 180°.
Order/compare several angles by eye before any measuring, so relative judgement (which is bigger) is trained alongside absolute estimation (how many degrees).
Use bodily and everyday referents — clock hands, opening doors, ramps, turns — to build the benchmark images.
keyRepresentations: Benchmark angles as mental anchors: 45°, 90° (right angle), 180° (straight), 270°, 360°
The right angle as the master reference ('a bit more / a bit less than a corner')
Reflex angle as 360° minus its companion angle (turn imagery)
Clock hands / opening door as dynamic referents for angle size
commonMisconceptions: Judges size by ray length rather than opening, so estimates a wide-but-short angle as smaller than a narrow-but-long one (arm-length carryover).
Has no reflex concept — sees a 270° reflex angle and reads/estimates the smaller 90° companion instead.
Anchors only to 90° and 180°, so estimates cluster at right angles and straight lines with poor resolution in between (e.g. calls everything obtuse '120°').
Treats 'estimate' as 'measure without care' and expects an exact answer rather than a reasoned approximate range.

learn.summary: Teach angle estimation as the sense-making partner of protractor measuring: the child judges an angle's size in degrees WITHOUT a tool by comparing it to internalised benchmarks (45°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). The goal is a stable mental image of a right angle, a straight angle and a three-quarter turn, so any angle can be placed relative to them ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°'). This extends acute/obtuse vocabulary to REFLEX angles (between 180° and 360°), met here for the first time and not directly readable on a semicircular protractor. Estimation makes measuring self-correcting: a child who expects 'about 130°' will not accept a protractor read of 50°.

activities.title: Predict-then-reveal angle estimation trainer
feedback: Reward closeness within a tolerance band rather than exactness, so an estimate stays a reasoned range, not a failed exact answer.

When a child guesses '90-ish' for a clearly reflex angle, reveal the turn swinging past the straight line and show its true size as 360° minus the companion angle (for example about 270° when the companion is about 90°), so reflex stops being invisible.

When a child under-estimates wide-but-short-armed angles, let the error score flag the pattern, then overlay the two angles vertex-to-vertex so their openings compare directly regardless of arm length, and extend the short arms and re-order to show the size is unchanged.
Treat a big estimate-vs-measure gap as a signal to recheck both the protractor reading (placement and scale) and the estimate, not simply to discard the estimate.
activities.rationale: Estimation is a perceptual-numerical skill proposed to be built by repeated visual trials with feedback: a predict-then-reveal loop over many varied angles commits the child to an estimate, then feeds back the error, intended to calibrate the benchmark sense. Varying ray length independently of opening directly targets the documented arm-length misconception; including reflex angles forces the '360 minus companion' reasoning that a semicircular protractor cannot read directly.
sourceClaims: Angle size is measured with reference to a circle whose whole is 360°; benchmark fractions of a turn (right angle = 90°, straight = 180°) anchor degree understanding, and an n-one-degree-angle turn measures n degrees (4.MD.5).

The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
Judging angle size by the length of the arms rather than the amount of opening is a persistent, documented misconception.
learnerActions: Look at an angle shown in a random orientation and, BEFORE any measuring, commit an estimate of its size in degrees (set a slider or type a number).
In ordering rounds, drag four angles into order from smallest to largest by eye before anything is measured.
Reveal the true measure and your error; when offered, fade in a faint benchmark 'ghost' (right-angle corner, or 180° straight line) over the angle to see how your estimate compared.
Meet angles whose ray (arm) lengths are varied at random so a wide angle sometimes has short arms — estimate by the opening, not the line length.
Meet reflex angles that swing past the straight line, and estimate them as 360° minus the smaller companion angle.
activities.intendedInsight: Any angle can be placed relative to a small set of benchmarks, and reflex angles (between 180° and 360°) are real angles estimated as 360° minus their companion — not the smaller angle on the other side.

activities.title: Scored estimation and classification practice
feedback: Score the slider estimate against a tolerance band so a near miss counts as success.
Flag an arm-length error when ordering tracks ray length rather than opening, and prompt direct comparison of the openings.
If the child mis-classifies the reflex angle as acute or right, show that it opens past the straight line.
activities.rationale: Estimation maps cleanly onto scored response formats (slider estimate, ordering, classification choice), giving varied practice and checking. A response-format task may give less rapid many-trial feedback than a live predict-reveal loop, so it is proposed as a complement rather than a replacement. Including a short-ray wide-angle item targets the arm-length misconception.
sourceClaims: Judging angle size by the length of the arms rather than the amount of opening is a persistent, documented misconception.

The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
learnerActions: Use a slider to estimate a shown angle's degrees, aiming to land within a tolerance band.
Order four angles smallest-to-largest by eye as an ordering task before any measure is shown.
Classify shown angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex, and pick out the reflex angle in a diagram.
Tackle at least one deliberately short-armed, wide-opening item designed to catch the arm-length habit.
activities.intendedInsight: Relative judgement (which is bigger), absolute estimation (how many degrees) and classification (acute/obtuse/reflex) are distinct skills that can each be practised and checked.

activities.title: Benchmark-angle gallery with everyday referents
feedback: Confirm the benchmark image and name when revealed, and connect it to its everyday referent.
When the child decides 'more or less than a right angle', show the angle against the corner image to confirm.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal gallery can seed estimation by anchoring the benchmark set as stable mental images with everyday referents. It is a scaffold: it may establish the anchors but does not itself run the estimate-check loop that calibrates estimation, so it is intended to precede, not replace, repeated estimation practice.
sourceClaims: Angle size is measured with reference to a circle whose whole is 360°; benchmark fractions of a turn (right angle = 90°, straight = 180°) anchor degree understanding, and an n-one-degree-angle turn measures n degrees (4.MD.5).
learnerActions: Tap or reveal each benchmark in turn — 45° (half a right angle), 90° (right angle/corner/quarter turn), 180° (straight), 270° (three right angles), 360° (full turn) — and link it to a reference image.
Connect each benchmark to a bodily or everyday referent: clock hands, an opening door, a ramp, a turn.
Use a lift-the-flap or 'more or less than a right angle?' layer to decide, for a shown angle, whether it is above or below the corner benchmark.
activities.intendedInsight: A small set of benchmark angles, anchored as physical and mental images, is the master reference set against which every other angle is judged ('a bit more / a bit less than a corner').

activities.title: Add intermediate anchors to sharpen resolution
feedback: If estimates snap only to 90° or 180°, point out the gap and introduce an intermediate anchor the angle sits near.
Accept a reasoned range stated against two anchors rather than demanding one exact number.
activities.rationale: When benchmark resolution is too coarse, estimates cluster at right angles and straight lines; this is a sparse-anchor-deployment issue, not a concept failure, so the fix is to bring in and practise intermediate anchors rather than reteach the concept of angle.
sourceClaims: The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
learnerActions: For a learner whose estimates snap only to 90° and 180°, bring in the half-right-angle (45°) and 'a right angle plus a third of a right angle' (120°) as working anchors alongside the secure 90° and 180° images.
Estimate angles that deliberately sit BETWEEN benchmarks, such as 60°, 110° or 130°, naming the two anchors each one falls between.
Justify at least one estimate aloud with benchmark language ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°').
activities.intendedInsight: Anchoring only to 90° and 180° makes estimates cluster there with poor resolution in between; deploying intermediate anchors gives the mental ruler finer gradations.

constraints: Always estimate BEFORE measuring, then measure to check; a large estimate-vs-measure gap signals that both should be rechecked (protractor placement and which scale was read, and the estimate itself), not that the estimate was worthless.
Reward closeness within a tolerance band, not exactness: an estimate is a reasoned approximate range, not a failed exact answer. An estimate of 120° when the protractor reads 128° is a good estimate.
A semicircular protractor reads only to 180°, so reflex angles must be reasoned as 360° minus the smaller companion angle; do not treat the smaller companion as the answer.

The benchmark gallery is a scaffold that anchors reference images; it may seed estimation but does not build the skill on its own, which requires repeated estimate-then-check trials. It is a useful precursor, not a universal requirement.

Classification and ordering response items check relative and absolute angle sense but, used alone, may give less rapid many-trial feedback than a live predict-reveal loop; combine formats rather than claiming any one medium is required.
Vary ray length independently of opening deliberately: wide-but-short-armed angles are the key trap for the arm-length misconception and should be included on purpose.

45° is part of the target benchmark set; the resolution-sharpening activity only re-deploys it for learners who have anchored to 90°/180° alone, and does not imply 45° is an optional extra for everyone.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The ±15° tolerance band and the specific benchmark set (45°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°) come from the legacy assessment and pedagogy fields; they are reasonable for ages 9–10 but are design choices, not values established by the cited sources.

The original pedagogy summary additionally lists 30° and 60° as benchmark angles, which its own keyRepresentations omits. This rewrite follows keyRepresentations: 30° is not carried through, and 60° appears only as an intermediate anchor in the resolution-sharpening activity. The inconsistency is inherited from the source and is not resolved by the cited references.

Legacy catalog rationales claiming a 3D environment 'adds spatial overhead without improving' estimation, that a character 'cannot show hundreds of angles', and that a static image 'cannot run the estimate-check loop' were medium-comparison statements; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, not asserted as universal pedagogical laws. A fixed image can still teach the benchmark set.

The sources support benchmark-degree reasoning and the arm-length misconception; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific interactive medium or the stated tolerance band. Efficacy-flavoured comparisons are stated with proposed/may wording only.

probeDeeper: Point to the short-armed wide angle and a long-armed narrow one: 'You said this one is smaller — what if I made its lines just as long as the other's? Would it still be smaller?' (counterexample: arm length is irrelevant.)
'How did you decide this one was about 130° — what did you compare it to?' — listen for a benchmark (right angle) rather than a guess.
'This reflex angle — how could you use the smaller angle next to it to work out its size?' (probes 360°-minus-companion reasoning.)
'Your estimate was 120° and the protractor says 128° — is your estimate wrong?' — checks the child understands an estimate is a reasoned range, not a failed exact answer.
assess.correctAnswer: Orders the four correctly by opening (not by arm length), estimates each within roughly ±15° of its true size, classifies the ~270° one as reflex (over a straight line, under a full turn) rather than reading its 90° companion, and uses benchmark language ('a bit more than a right angle') to justify at least one estimate.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders by arm length not opening — puts the short-armed wide angle earlier (smaller) than a long-armed narrow one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the two angles vertex-to-vertex so the openings compare directly regardless of arm length; extend the short arms and re-order to show the size is unchanged.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ordering tracks ray length rather than degrees; the child may point to the longer lines as the reason it's 'bigger'.

errorPatterns.pattern: No reflex concept — estimates the ~270° reflex angle as its ~90° companion, or as 'about 90°', reading the wrong side of the opening.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the turn dynamically past the straight line; estimate reflex as 360° minus the companion; explicitly name 'reflex: more than 180°, less than 360°'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the reflex angle acute/right or gives a sub-180° number; treats the reflex mark as if it were the smaller angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Benchmark resolution too coarse — snaps every estimate to 90° or 180°, so a 130° angle is called '90' or '180' with nothing in between.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the half-right-angle (45°) and 'a bit past a right angle' (~120°) as extra anchors; practise estimating angles that sit between benchmarks. No reteaching of concept — the anchor set is just sparse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Estimates cluster only at right angles and straight lines; no use of 45°/60°/120° as intermediate anchors.

responseLevels.gap: Estimates bear little relation to actual size and ordering follows arm length or orientation; no benchmark reasoning and no reflex concept (reads reflex as its companion).
responseLevels.full: Orders all four by opening regardless of arm length, estimates each within about ±15° using benchmark comparisons including intermediate anchors, correctly identifies and estimates the reflex angle via 360°-minus-companion, and treats the estimate as a reasoned range confirmed (not replaced) by measuring.
responseLevels.partial: Estimates acute and obtuse angles reasonably against 90°/180° and orders standard angles correctly, but is caught by at least one of: the short-arm wide angle (orders by length), the reflex angle (no over-180° concept), or coarse resolution (snaps to 90/180). Can name benchmarks but not deploy intermediate ones.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out four angles the child can see but not measure — include one clearly acute (~40°), one obtuse (~130°), one drawn with short arms but a wide opening, and one reflex (~270°), with ray lengths deliberately uneven. Say: 'Without measuring, put these in order from smallest to largest, and tell me roughly how many degrees each one is.' Then let them measure to check. Watch the ordering and the estimates — do not coach.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The uneven ray lengths separate opening-based judgement from arm-length judgement; the short-arm wide angle is the trap. The reflex angle separates a child who has extended their concept past 180° from one who collapses it back to the acute companion. Ordering plus numeric estimate together expose both relative and absolute angle sense in one two-minute task.
